question:
A recurring workflow in our team passes work from one person to the next, and today only two senior developers know how it goes. I want to write it down so that new developers and automated coding agents follow it the same way every time: what must the write-up state, and in what forms can it be written?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:

## What the Write-Up Must State

**1. State the purpose and intended outcomes of the workflow.**
A process description must cover its purpose and outcomes — these are the foundational elements that explain why the workflow exists and what it is meant to achieve.

The write-up must decompose the workflow into activities (sets of cohesive tasks) and tasks (required, recommended, or permissible actions intended to contribute to outcomes). **8. Build in process-monitoring hooks so the workflow can be assessed and improved.**

## In What Forms Can It Be Written?

### Summary

In short, your write-up must cover: **purpose, outcomes, activities, tasks, inputs, outputs, roles/actors, controls, enabling resources, training provisions, and monitoring/improvement criteria**. It can be expressed in any combination of **prose (unstructured or structured), use-case templates, flowcharts, activity diagrams, sequence diagrams, data flow diagrams, decision tables,** and ultimately **automation scripts** — with more formal notations producing less ambiguity and being more directly usable by automated coding agents.
